extracted.intended_audience: startup founders and small PR teams seeking media coverage from tech and business reporters
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for founders/early-stage companies on how to pitch journalists and get media coverage, including timing, content, contact method, and relationship-building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the reporter/publication's preferred contact channel
rubrics_metrics.description: Most publications and individual journalists have explicit preferred ways to be contacted (intake/contact forms, author pages, Twitter/LinkedIn, email listed on author pages). You don't need to guess.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Coindesk has a detailed intake form; Axios email addresses are listed on author pages or bios; reporters often publish preferred contact info. Follow that guidance rather than inventing a contact path.

rubrics_metrics.name: Send a direct, tailored pitch
rubrics_metrics.description: Always send a direct, tailored pitch to the reporter, customized to them and the publication rather than a generic blast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sean Silcoff: 'always a direct, tailored pitch'; Clark Kent: direct outreach establishes a personal relationship and cuts through PR noise. Avoid generic mass-sends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer email when a reporter requests it
rubrics_metrics.description: Some reporters prefer email because it lets them read, research and evaluate on their own time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aleksandra Sagan (The Logic) explicitly prefers email over a phone call. If a reporter states a preference for email, follow it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early-stage founders should reach out directly (not necessarily via PR firm)
rubrics_metrics.description: For early-stage startups, direct contact (email/DM) from founders is often better than going through a PR agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clark Kent: direct outreach builds personal relationships and cuts through PR inbox clutter; Kia Kokalitcheva: founders can usually manage outreach themselves if they follow good communications practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitch actual news — be newsworthy
rubrics_metrics.description: Pitches must contain real news: significant deals, timely trends, major hires/founders, or developments that matter to readers — not generic self-promotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kia Kokalitcheva: 'Actual news!' Examples of non-news: website redesigns, routine headcount milestones, minor rebrands unless you're a top consumer brand. Significant examples given: Mindbridge Series A (AI for auditors) was interesting because it could transform a profession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit the publication and reporter's beat
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure your story aligns with what the publication and specific reporter cover; tailor the pitch to their beats and readership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doug Soltys: understand what BetaKit covers; Aleksandra Sagan: reporters cover specific beats (e.g., e-commerce, B.C.) — show you know the type of stories The Logic writes. Sean Silcoff: focus on what readers would find interesting.

rubrics_metrics.name: State who is involved and why it matters (the 'who' and the 'why')
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly explain who is doing the thing (founder pedigree, players involved) and why it matters in concrete, non-marketing terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clark Kent: founder pedigree matters for vetting pre-traction announcements; the 'why' should be stated plainly rather than marketing-speak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do your homework on the reporter and publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Research the reporter's past work and the publication's lens so you can craft a targeted, relevant pitch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: William Johnson: read what the reporter has written; Kia: reach the right reporter who focuses on your sector/type of news; Doug: be prepared with a storytelling data room before outreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow up reasonably but don't be overbearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow-ups increase the chance a busy reporter will see your pitch, but excessive pressure or harassment is damaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: William Johnson: reporters get hundreds of emails; follow up if you don’t hear back (48+ hours isn't definitive). Kia and others warn against following up too much or trying to pressure/control the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write clear, concise emails without jargon or marketing-speak
rubrics_metrics.description: Pitch emails should be short, direct, and free of nonsense jargon, with key logistical details included (type of news, target date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kia: include key information like type of news, target date; keep copy clear. Avoid flowery marketing language that obscures the substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have assets and your story ready before pitching
rubrics_metrics.description: Be prepared with all necessary assets, data, and messaging — don't try to assemble materials after outreach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doug Soltys: have a storytelling data room and all required assets ready; make it very easy for the journalist to opt in and get started immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offering an exclusive can improve interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Offering an exclusive to a reporter/outlet can make the pitch more enticing, though it's not a guarantee of coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kia: pitching news that would be exclusive to the outlet is a great way to be enticing, especially for standalone stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give journalists adequate lead time depending on story type
rubrics_metrics.description: Timing depends on the type of coverage: standalone feature stories typically need about a week; deal/newsletter items may be ok with a day or less; more time is preferred for editing and fact-checking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kia: ~1 week is the sweet spot for standalone stories; day-before can work for deal sections. Aleksandra: farther in advance is better due to editing and fact-checking. Doug: time is your ally — don't expect coverage in 48 hours for complex stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: PR firms can help but are not a guarantee
rubrics_metrics.description: A PR firm can add value via relationships, pitching expertise, and strategy — but they are not necessary in many cases and may be ineffective if poorly chosen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kia: short answer no — founders can often do it themselves; Sean: there are many bad PR firms; William: firms can help if they have relationships; Doug: vet agencies — some have proven value; Aleksandra: a well-crafted pitch can come from anyone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't lie or mislead
rubrics_metrics.description: Dishonesty destroys credibility and future chances of coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kia and Doug: 'Lying: don't do it, we never forget' and 'Don't lie to us or feed us a line.' Being untruthful will ruin relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't pitch multiple reporters at the same publication (unless guided)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid sending the same pitch to several reporters at a single outlet — reporters coordinate and mass-pitches are annoying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sean Silcoff: 'Don’t pitch multiple reporters at the same publication.' If one reporter passes and suggests someone else, follow that guidance rather than blind-mass emailing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect editorial independence (no gifts/quid pro quo)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of and respect the publication's editorial independence policies (no gifts or attempts to influence coverage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aleksandra Sagan: The Logic has a strict editorial independence policy and does not accept gifts; understand outlet policies before engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid being pushy, cagey, or overly controlling
rubrics_metrics.description: Pushiness, hostility, withholding key information, or trying to control the story undermines relationships and future coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clark Kent: being pushy or cagey ruins chances; after publication, repeatedly demanding corrections or complaining about tone will destroy future coverage prospects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide compelling, business-focused substance (phenomenal raw materials)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists are looking for compelling material that makes for a strong story — emphasize business impact, scalability, and why readers should care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: William Johnson: 'We’re in the business of crafting compelling stories — give us phenomenal raw materials'; Doug: emphasize how innovation will scale the business, as business publications care about scaling and commercial impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand each publication's lens and audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Different outlets will interpret the same story differently; match your pitch to the publication's perspective and audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doug: different publications see stories through different lenses; understand which outlets care about certain aspects of your story and pitch accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be interesting and have a hook (personality can help)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even founder energy or genuine personality can be a hook; there must be something that grabs the reporter — substance or distinctiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clark Kent: you or the idea must be interesting; sometimes founder energy or authenticity is the hook. Sean: a 'no' now isn't necessarily permanent — persistence and timing matter.
